entities.rationale: Rich, very well governed and water-secure, so local collapse is unlikely; the main local risk is a war with Russia on its long border. Near-free essentials need superintelligence, because an ageing population keeps health costs high.

Recurring civil war, a very weak state, widespread hunger and fast population growth make a renewed country-wide breakdown in security or food quite likely. Abundance would need outside abundance spreading in, which is only plausible with superintelligence.

Water depends entirely on desalination and food mostly on imports, with extreme heat, the Gulf war risk and the end of oil revenues as the stresses. Cheap solar power makes desalination and cooling affordable if the economy adapts.

A peaceful, wealthy island where global doom is the main collapse path; its heavy reliance on energy imports is the main local weakness. Its very high income makes the under-10% cost test easier to pass than for most countries.

EU and NATO membership protects it, but it borders Ukraine, depends on imported energy and has middling governance. Abundance tracks how quickly superintelligence-driven productivity reaches Central Europe.

Gaza's essentials have already broken down, and a lasting escalation in the West Bank would push a majority of Palestinians past the collapse line. Occupation, water scarcity and dependence on outside supplies leave little control over the essentials.
Remote, peaceful, a food exporter with plenty of water and renewable power, so global doom is almost the only path to collapse. Earthquakes and volcanoes are the local tail risks.
A Sahel desert country exposed to drought, food shortages and spillover from Mali's jihadist wars, with weak state capacity. Its large solar and hydrogen potential is the main path upward.

A stable democracy with a renewable grid and good health outcomes; rising drug violence and a heavy interest bill are the main local stresses. Abundance needs superintelligence to raise incomes well beyond the middle range.

Rich, but it relies on desalinated water, imported food and air conditioning in some of the world's hottest summers, beside Iraq and Iran. The oil revenues that pay for its subsidies are likely to shrink by 2100.

Fairly rich and stable, but interest takes almost 30% of state revenue, the country is very unequal, and droughts already threaten the canal's water supply. These limit how cheap the essentials can become.

Russia occupies part of its territory and invaded in 2008, and domestic politics are unstable, so security is the main collapse risk. Life expectancy is near the 75-year line and many people lack safe water.

EU, eurozone and NATO membership and ample water make local collapse unlikely; rapid ageing and imported energy are the main pressures. Abundance depends on superintelligence making health care and energy cheap.
A closed, repressive state with indefinite conscription, a live risk of war with Ethiopia over sea access, and drought-prone farming. Food and security are the most likely essentials to fail.

Bitter winters make heating essential, safe water reaches fewer than half of residents, and the country sits between Russia and China. Mining wealth and a stable democracy help, but governance is weak.
Very stable politics, a renewable grid and large food surpluses make collapse unlikely; rising crime and droughts like Montevideo's 2023 water crisis are the weak points.

The US connection gives a strong backstop and access to US abundance if it comes, but the fragile grid, stronger hurricanes, a shrinking and ageing population and past bankruptcy make long energy failures the main risk.
Ethnic divisions and secession pressure from Republika Srpska keep a security breakdown possible, and emigration and ageing weaken the state. A path to the EU is its main stabiliser.

Peaceful and fairly well run, but it is one of Africa's driest countries, with frequent droughts, widespread hunger and low life expectancy, so water and food are the weak essentials. Its solar and hydrogen potential is a real upside.
Hostile neighbours and the 2023 loss of Nagorno-Karabakh make security the dominant risk, even with the 2025 peace framework. Imported energy, high water stress and a heavy interest bill add strain.
